Input type: legacy `.crash` text report, single crash, symbolicated, complete.

## 1. What happened

Chartwright quit immediately after starting up because macOS decided one of the app's own bundled components had been altered and refused to trust it. The system shut the app down rather than let the untrusted code run.

## 2. The core issue

The app called `dlopen()` (a runtime request to load a library on demand) for its embedded framework `NGPlotEngine`, and the kernel rejected the file's code signature (the cryptographic seal that proves a binary hasn't been modified since it was built). The Application Specific Information block states this directly: `code signature invalid (errno=1)` for `/Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework/Versions/A/NGPlotEngine`. `Termination Reason: CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page` narrows it further — a specific memory page of that binary failed its hash check, meaning the on-disk bytes no longer match what the signature covers. Exception Type `EXC_CRASH (SIGKILL (Code Signature Invalid))` confirms macOS killed the process outright rather than returning an error to the app. The signature blob is present and located (`codeBlobOffset=0x0041C000, codeBlobSize=0x00009B40`), so this is a content mismatch, not a missing signature.

Alternative reading: the framework file is truncated or corrupted on disk (partial download, bad copy, or damaged installer) rather than deliberately modified — would be confirmed by running `codesign -vvv --deep` on the framework and comparing its size/hash against a known-good build.

## 3. Why it happened

The most common source of `CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page` on a nested framework is a build or distribution step that touched the binary *after* it was signed — for example running `install_name_tool`, `strip`, a resource copy, or a notarization-stapling script against the framework once its signature was already applied. Signing order matters: nested code inside `Contents/Frameworks/` must be signed before the outer `.app` bundle, and any edit afterward invalidates it. The report shows this Mac runs `macOS 15.5 (24F74)` with `System Integrity Protection: enabled`, and `Code Type: ARM-64 (Native)` on Apple Silicon — where code signature enforcement is mandatory for every executable page, not advisory as it once was on Intel. Nothing here points to an OS version or architecture mismatch: the app is a native arm64 build and the framework was found on disk at the expected path. Only the outer app, `dyld` (the dynamic linker, the part of macOS that loads libraries), and AppKit appear in Binary Images — `NGPlotEngine` never mapped, so it never got that far.

## 4. Why it crashed this way

This was a runtime failure a fraction of a second into launch, not a link-time one. Frame 5 is `CWAppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:)`, so the app had fully started, loaded AppKit, and reached its delegate callback — frame 6 is AppKit's `-[NSApplication _postDidFinishNotification]`. Frame 4, `NGPluginHost.loadRenderer()`, is the app's own code deciding to pull in the plugin framework at that moment. That call lands in `dyld4::APIs::dlopen_from` (frame 3), which means the framework was loaded dynamically at runtime rather than linked at launch — had it been a normal link-time dependency, the failure would have appeared before `main` ran. Frames 2 through 0 walk down into `dyld4::JustInTimeLoader::makeLaunchLoader`, `dyld4::Loader::mapSegments`, and finally `SyscallDelegate::mapFileReadable`, which is the exact point where dyld asks the kernel to map the framework's pages into memory. That mapping is where signature enforcement bites: on Apple Silicon each page is hash-verified as it is faulted in, so the failure surfaces at map time, not at open time. Exception Codes are `0x0` / `0x0` and Exception Note is `EXC_CORPSE_NOTIFY`, consistent with a kernel-initiated kill that left a corpse for the reporter rather than an application-generated fault. Because the kill is `SIGKILL`, the app got no chance to catch an error and fall back — `dlopen()` never returned, so any error-handling branch in `loadRenderer()` was unreachable. Thread 0 is the only thread listed and is the triggering thread, matching a single-threaded startup path.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)

1. Verify the shipped framework first to confirm the diagnosis:
   ```
   codesign -vvv --deep --strict /Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   spctl -a -vvv -t exec /Applications/Chartwright.app
   ```
2. Audit the build pipeline for any step that modifies `NGPlotEngine` after signing — `install_name_tool`, `strip`, `lipo`, `dsymutil`, resource copies, or a custom Run Script phase. Move all such edits *before* the signing step.
3. Sign inside-out, nested code first, then the outer bundle:
   ```
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     -s "Developer ID Application: ..." \
     Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework/Versions/A
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     -s "Developer ID Application: ..." Chartwright.app
   ```
4. In Xcode, leave "Code Sign On Copy" enabled for `NGPlotEngine.framework` in the Embed Frameworks phase, and remove any manual post-embed signing that duplicates it.
5. Notarize and staple the finished `.app`, not the framework alone, then re-verify with `spctl` before shipping — this catches invalidation introduced by packaging or the installer.
6. Make `loadRenderer()` resilient where it can be: prefer link-time embedding for a first-party framework, or if `dlopen()` must stay, log the framework's `codesign` status at startup so field reports show the mismatch before the kill.

## 6. The fix (user-side)

1. Delete Chartwright from `/Applications` (drag it to the Trash and empty it) — do not just copy a new copy over the old one, since a partially damaged file can survive that.
2. Download a fresh copy from the vendor's official page or the Mac App Store, and let the download finish completely before opening it.
3. Reinstall and launch. If it crashes again with the same message, the vendor's build itself is broken — report the version, `11.3.0 (11300)`, and your macOS version, `15.5 (24F74)`, to their support.
4. If the app came from a shared drive, USB stick, or a file-sync folder, install instead from the original download — copies through those channels can be altered in transit.

Security note: do not disable System Integrity Protection or Gatekeeper to work around this; the signature rejection is macOS correctly detecting that a component does not match what its developer signed.

## 1. What happened
Chartwright shut down immediately during startup because macOS decided one of the app's own bundled components had been altered and could no longer be trusted. The system killed the app rather than let the modified component run.

## 2. The core issue
macOS verified the code signature (a cryptographic seal Apple requires on executables, covering the file page by page) of the app's embedded framework and found a mismatch. `Termination Reason: CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page` means a memory page loaded from disk did not match the hash recorded in the signature. The Application Specific Information block names the file precisely: `/Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework/Versions/A/NGPlotEngine`, with `code signature invalid (errno=1)`. Because the mismatch is per-page rather than a rejected certificate, the most likely cause is that the framework binary's bytes were changed after it was signed, leaving a stale seal. Alternative reading: on-disk corruption of that one framework from a failed download or update — would be confirmed by comparing the file's checksum against a fresh copy from the vendor, or by `codesign -v --verbose=4` on the framework reporting a specific invalid page rather than a signing-identity error.

## 3. Why it happened
The signature covers the exact bytes of `NGPlotEngine`; anything that rewrites those bytes after `codesign` runs invalidates it. Common triggers are post-signing build steps (`install_name_tool`, `strip`, resource copying) executed after the signing phase, or an updater that patches the framework in place inside `/Applications`. The main executable itself was fine — frames 5 through 7 show the app's own code (`main`, `CWAppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:)`) running normally before the failure, so only the embedded framework's seal is broken. `System Integrity Protection: enabled` and `OS Version: macOS 15.5 (24F74)` confirm a stock, fully enforcing system. Nothing in the report points to an architecture problem: `Code Type: ARM-64 (Native)` matches the arm64 addresses throughout.

## 4. Why it crashed this way
This was a launch-time failure, not a runtime one. Frame 5 is `CWAppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:)`, called from AppKit's `-[NSApplication _postDidFinishNotification]` at frame 6 — so the app died in its very first delegate callback. Frame 4, `NGPluginHost.loadRenderer()`, called into `dyld4::APIs::dlopen_from` (frame 3) — `dlopen` is the call that loads a library on demand rather than at launch, which is why the failure surfaces inside app code instead of before `main`. dyld (the dynamic linker, the part of macOS that maps libraries into a process) then reached `dyld4::Loader::mapSegments` (frame 1) and `SyscallDelegate::mapFileReadable` (frame 0), where the kernel maps the framework's pages into memory. At that point the kernel validated each page against the signature, hit a mismatch, and refused. `Exception Type: EXC_CRASH (SIGKILL (Code Signature Invalid))` is the result: SIGKILL is an unblockable termination signal, so there was no chance for the app to catch an error or show a dialog. `Exception Codes: 0x0...0, 0x0...0` carry no extra detail, consistent with a policy kill rather than a memory fault. The report's `codeBlobOffset=0x0041C000, codeBlobSize=0x00009B40` locate the signature blob inside the framework binary, confirming a signature was present — it simply did not match the file contents. `Triggered by Thread: 0` and `Crashed Thread: 0` place everything on the main thread, exactly where a synchronous plugin load during launch would run.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)
1. Move every binary-modifying step — `install_name_tool`, `strip`, `lipo`, resource injection — to run **before** signing. Any of them after `codesign` breaks the seal.
2. Sign inside-out: embedded frameworks first, then the app bundle.
   ```
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     --sign "Developer ID Application: Northgate" \
     Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     --sign "Developer ID Application: Northgate" Chartwright.app
   ```
3. In Xcode, confirm the Embed Frameworks build phase has **Code Sign On Copy** checked for `NGPlotEngine.framework`, and that it runs before any custom Run Script phases that touch binaries.
4. Verify before shipping:
   ```
   codesign -vvv --deep --strict Chartwright.app
   spctl -a -vv -t exec Chartwright.app
   ```
5. Notarize (Apple's automated malware scan, required for distribution outside the App Store) and staple the ticket to the whole bundle, then distribute as a signed DMG or pkg so no post-install step rewrites files in place.
6. Audit the updater: if it patches files inside `/Applications/Chartwright.app`, replace it with whole-bundle atomic replacement, since in-place patching invalidates the signature.

## 6. The fix (user-side)
1. Drag `/Applications/Chartwright.app` to the Trash, empty it, then download and install a fresh copy from Northgate's official site — this replaces the damaged component.
2. If the download was interrupted or came from a file-sharing service, download again from the vendor directly and let it finish completely before installing.
3. Run **Disk Utility > First Aid** on your startup disk to rule out storage corruption, then reinstall once more.
4. If it still quits at launch, send this crash report to Northgate support and quote `CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page` and `NGPlotEngine` — it likely needs a corrected build from them.

## 2. The core issue

macOS could not validate the code signature (the cryptographic seal Apple requires on executable code) of the app's bundled framework at `/Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework/Versions/A/NGPlotEngine`. The `Application Specific Information` block states it plainly: `code signature invalid (errno=1)`, with a code blob at `codeBlobOffset=0x0041C000`. `Termination Reason: CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page` means a memory page loaded from that file did not match the hash recorded in its signature — the file's bytes differ from what was signed. Alternative reading: the framework was signed correctly but modified after signing — by a build step, an installer, a disk-repair/antivirus tool, or file corruption — which would be confirmed by running `codesign -vvv --deep` on the installed bundle and comparing its `CDHash` to the shipped build.

## 3. Why it happened

- The framework is loaded lazily, not at launch: frame 3 is `dyld4::APIs::dlopen_from` (dyld is the dynamic linker, the part of macOS that maps shared libraries into a running process), called from `NGPluginHost.loadRenderer()` at frame 4. A signature problem in a framework loaded this way is not caught until that moment.
- `System Integrity Protection: enabled` and macOS 15.5 (24F74) mean signature enforcement is fully active; on Apple Silicon (`Code Type: ARM-64 (Native)`) all executable code must carry a valid signature — there is no unsigned fallback.
- The specific failure is page-level, not "missing signature," which points to content drift between signing time and load time rather than an unsigned binary.

## 4. Why it crashed this way

- No crash occurred in the ordinary sense of a bad pointer: `Exception Codes: 0x0000000000000000, 0x0000000000000000` and `Exception Note: EXC_CORPSE_NOTIFY` indicate the kernel terminated the process and produced a corpse report, rather than the app faulting on its own.
- The kill arrived during page mapping. Frame 0 is `dyld4::SyscallDelegate::mapFileReadable`, frame 1 `dyld4::Loader::mapSegments` — dyld was mapping the framework's segments into memory when the kernel validated a page against the signature and rejected it.
- This is why the report says `Invalid Page` rather than a load-failure error: signature hashes are checked per page as pages are faulted in, so the process dies mid-map instead of receiving a clean `dlopen` failure it could report to the user.
- Timing is launch-adjacent but not launch-blocking: frame 5 is `CWAppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:)`, reached via `-[NSApplication _postDidFinishNotification]` (frame 6). The app fully initialized, AppKit posted its finished-launching notification, and only then did the plugin load run.
- `Time Awake Since Boot: 9400 seconds` confirms this was a normal user launch on a running system, not a boot-time or install-time event.
- Only the main thread is involved — `Crashed Thread: 0`, `Triggered by Thread: 0` — consistent with synchronous plugin loading on the main thread.
- The `Binary Images` table lists only `Chartwright`, `dyld`, and `AppKit`; `NGPlotEngine` is absent, confirming it never finished mapping.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)

1. Reproduce and read the exact verdict on the installed copy:
   ```
   codesign -vvv --deep --strict /Applications/Chartwright.app
   codesign -dvvv /Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   spctl -a -vvv -t exec /Applications/Chartwright.app
   ```
2. Sign inside-out: every nested framework must be signed **before** the outer app, and nothing may touch the files afterward. Any post-signing step (strip, install_name_tool, resource copy, chmod, plist edit) invalidates the seal and produces exactly this `Invalid Page` result.
3. Move `NGPlotEngine.framework` embedding into a proper *Embed Frameworks* build phase with **Code Sign On Copy** enabled, rather than a hand-rolled Copy Files or shell script phase.
4. Re-sign with the same identity and the hardened runtime, then re-verify:
   ```
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     --sign "Developer ID Application: Northgate" \
     Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     --sign "Developer ID Application: Northgate" Chartwright.app
   ```
5. Notarize and staple the shipped artifact (`xcrun notarytool submit`, then `xcrun stapler staple`), and confirm the staple survives your DMG/PKG packaging step — repackaging after stapling is a common way to reintroduce this.
6. Make the failure survivable: wrap `NGPluginHost.loadRenderer()` so a plugin that fails to load degrades to a fallback path. Note that `SIGKILL` cannot be caught, so the real protection is verifying the framework's signature before `dlopen`, or shipping the renderer as a separate XPC/helper process.

## 6. The fix (user-side)

1. Delete `/Applications/Chartwright.app` by dragging it to the Trash, then download a fresh copy directly from Northgate's official site and reinstall. A partially-copied or damaged install causes this exact error.
2. Do not open the app bundle and add, remove, or replace files inside `Contents/Frameworks` — modifying anything in there breaks the app's seal and macOS will refuse to run it.
3. If you use antivirus, "app cleaner," or disk-optimizer utilities, exclude `/Applications/Chartwright.app` from them; some of these rewrite files inside apps and invalidate the signature.
4. If a clean reinstall still fails, send Northgate support this crash report and mention `CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page` for `NGPlotEngine` — that indicates a problem with the build they shipped, which only they can correct.

## 1. What happened
PhotoEditor froze for about 6.4 seconds while opening a document, and its window stopped responding during that time. The app did not quit or crash — it was simply stuck waiting.

## 2. The core issue
The main thread (the single thread that draws the UI and handles clicks; if it is busy, the app appears frozen) was parked in `__psynch_cvwait` — the kernel call that blocks a thread on a condition variable (a lock-style signal one thread uses to wait until another thread says "done"). It got there from `-[PERenderQueue waitForPendingTiles] + 96`, meaning the app deliberately told the UI thread to stop and wait for image tiles to finish rendering. The thread that was supposed to signal it, `PERenderWorker`, sat in `read + 8` inside `libsystem_kernel.dylib`, called from `-[PETileRenderer renderTile:] + 2208` — that is, blocked reading data from a file descriptor. So the UI was held hostage by a worker thread doing slow I/O. All 64 of 64 samples show both threads in the same frames, so neither made progress during the entire sampled window.

## 3. Why it happened
The design couples document opening to tile rendering synchronously: `-[PEDocumentController openDocumentAtURL:]` calls straight into `-[PERenderQueue waitForPendingTiles]` on `com.apple.main-thread`. That is only safe if rendering is fast, and here it was not, because `PERenderWorker` was blocked in `read` rather than computing. A `read` that stalls for seconds usually means the bytes are coming from something slower than local flash — a network volume, an external or sleeping disk, or a very large file being pulled in one pass. Nothing in this report identifies the file or volume, so the source of the slow read is not established. There is no sign of a system-level fault: `Duration: 6.42s` and `Steps: 64` describe a stall, not a failure.

## 4. Why it crashed this way
No crash occurred — this is a hang report, so there is no faulting thread, signal, or termination reason to explain. The failure mode is a stall of `6.42s` (`Duration`), sampled across `64` steps at a 100 ms interval, with every sample showing the same stack. Thread `0x1f4a21`, labelled `DispatchQueue "com.apple.main-thread"`, is the one macOS watches for responsiveness, which is why the freeze was user-visible: its innermost frame is `__psynch_cvwait + 8` in `libsystem_kernel.dylib`, a voluntary wait rather than a spin, so CPU use would have been near zero while the beachball showed. Below it sits the normal AppKit event loop (`-[NSApplication run] + 512`), confirming the app was fully launched and in steady-state runtime, not launching. Thread `0x1f4a55`, `"PERenderWorker"`, is also blocked all 64 samples, in `read + 8`. Because the waiter and the worker are both blocked, the app was making no forward progress at all for the sampled duration. The report ends after `Binary Images`, so whether the hang resolved after 6.4 s or continued is not recorded.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)
1. Remove the blocking wait from the UI path — `-[PEDocumentController openDocumentAtURL:]` should return immediately and let tiles arrive asynchronously:
   ```objc
   [self.renderQueue renderTilesForURL:url completion:^(PETileSet *tiles) {
       dispatch_async(dispatch_get_main_queue(), ^{ [self presentTiles:tiles]; });
   }];
   ```
2. Show placeholder/progressive tiles while rendering completes, instead of holding the main thread in `waitForPendingTiles`.
3. If a wait is unavoidable, bound it and fall back rather than blocking indefinitely on the condition variable.
4. Fix the worker stall in `-[PETileRenderer renderTile:]`: read in chunks, memory-map large files, and treat network/external volumes as slow paths.
5. Add a main-thread watchdog assertion in debug builds so any blocking call on `com.apple.main-thread` fails loudly in testing.
6. Reproduce and verify with Instruments (Time Profiler plus File Activity) against a file on a slow or network volume, then re-sample:
   ```
   sample PhotoEditor 10 -file /tmp/photoeditor-sample.txt
   ```

## 6. The fix (user-side)
1. Wait a few seconds — this was a temporary freeze, not a crash; the app recovered rather than quitting.
2. If it happens when opening a specific image, copy that file to your local `Downloads` folder and open it from there, rather than from a network share, NAS, or external drive.
3. Make sure external drives are awake and connected, and that any cloud folder (iCloud Drive, Dropbox) has finished downloading the file locally before opening it.
4. Check for an app update from the developer, and report the freeze with the file's size and where it was stored.

## 1. What happened
The app froze for about 6.4 seconds while opening a document, leaving the window unresponsive to clicks and typing. It did not crash — it was still running, just stuck waiting for image tiles to finish.

## 2. The core issue
The main thread (the one that draws the interface and handles input) parked itself in `__psynch_cvwait` — a kernel call that sleeps a thread until another thread signals a condition variable (a lock-based "wake me when you're done" primitive). The frame above it, `-[PERenderQueue waitForPendingTiles] + 96`, shows the app deliberately blocking the interface until rendering completes. Meanwhile the worker thread named `PERenderWorker` sits in `read + 8` inside `libsystem_kernel.dylib`, i.e. blocked on a file read that has not returned. So the wait is legitimate but unbounded: the main thread cannot wake until the worker finishes I/O, and the worker is stalled in the kernel. All 64 samples show identical stacks, so neither thread advanced during the entire sampled window.

Alternative reading: a lost-wakeup or missed-signal deadlock in `PERenderQueue` rather than slow I/O — would be confirmed by a longer sample or spindump showing whether `read` ever returns and whether the worker's sample count keeps growing on the same frame indefinitely.

## 3. Why it happened
`-[PEDocumentController openDocumentAtURL:] + 640` calls `waitForPendingTiles` directly on `com.apple.main-thread`, so document opening was designed as a synchronous, blocking operation. That is safe only when the underlying work is fast and bounded; here it depends on `read` completing in `-[PETileRenderer renderTile:] + 2208`, which is unbounded — a large file, a slow or sleeping external disk, or a network volume all stretch it arbitrarily. Nothing in this report indicates a code signing (Apple's binary-authenticity checks), entitlement (per-app permission grants), or architecture problem: the process is `arm64e` on `Mac15,7` running macOS 15.5 (24F74), and its own binary plus AppKit and `libsystem_kernel.dylib` all loaded normally.

## 4. Why it crashed this way
No crash occurred — this is a hang, and the process was alive throughout. `Duration: 6.42s` with `Steps: 64 (100ms sampling interval)` means the sampler took 64 snapshots and reported the same stack for all of them, which is why the header calls it the "Heaviest stack for the main thread." A responsive app would show varied frames across samples; a single unchanging stack for the full window is the signature of a block, not slow work. The blocking frame is thread `0x1f4a21`, `DispatchQueue "com.apple.main-thread"`, at frame 6, `__psynch_cvwait + 8 (libsystem_kernel.dylib + 15112)`. Because AppKit's event loop (`-[NSApplication run] + 512`) is three frames below the wait, no user events were being dispatched, which is what the user perceives as a frozen window. The `PERenderWorker` thread (`0x1f4a55`, priority 33) is likewise pinned at `read + 8` for all 64 samples, so it never signalled the condition the main thread was waiting on. The hang ended at `10:02:17.8610`, roughly 6.4 s after it began, so the read did eventually complete or time out — consistent with slow I/O rather than a permanent deadlock, though the sample alone cannot settle that.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)
1. Stop blocking the main thread in `openDocumentAtURL:` — return immediately, show placeholder or progress UI, and update when tiles arrive.
2. Move the wait off the main thread and deliver results asynchronously:
   ```swift
   renderQueue.renderTiles(for: url) { [weak self] tiles in
       DispatchQueue.main.async { self?.present(tiles) }
   }
   ```
3. Give `waitForPendingTiles` a bounded wait and a failure path instead of an infinite condition wait, so a stalled `read` degrades into an error rather than a freeze.
4. Make `-[PETileRenderer renderTile:]` cancellable and I/O-aware — check for cancellation between reads, and read in chunks so a slow volume yields progress.
5. Add a main-thread watchdog in debug builds (assert if any main-thread wait exceeds ~100 ms) to catch regressions before shipping.
6. Reproduce against a slow or network volume and re-sample with `sample PhotoEditor 10 -file /tmp/pe.txt` to confirm the main thread no longer reaches `__psynch_cvwait`.

## 6. The fix (user-side)
1. Wait a few seconds — this hang lasted about 6.4 seconds and cleared on its own; force-quitting is usually unnecessary.
2. Copy the document to your internal drive and open it from there, since the stall was in a file read that may involve an external, sleeping, or network disk.
3. If it involves a network or cloud folder, make sure the file is fully downloaded locally before opening it.
4. Check for an app update in the App Store or from the developer, and report that PhotoEditor 5.1 (510) hangs when opening documents on macOS 15.5.
